content.p: On the afternoon of 4 August 2022 a Mercedes-Benz ran a red light at La Brea and Slauson avenues in Windsor Hills, a community in southwest Los Angeles County, at a speed prosecutors later put at 130 miles per hour. It hit cross traffic, cars burst into flames, and six people died: a pregnant woman, her unborn son, her 11-month-old boy, her boyfriend, and two women in another car. The driver was Nicole Lorraine Linton, a travelling nurse from Houston who had left her hospital shift that afternoon.

More than four years later, on 2 October 2026, a Los Angeles jury convicted Linton of six counts of second-degree murder after about three hours of deliberation. The trial had turned on one question. Prosecutors said she was conscious, angry and in control of the car. Her lawyers said she had suffered a seizure.

The speed limit on that stretch of La Brea Avenue is 35 miles per hour. Surveillance video, parts of which were played to the jury, showed the Mercedes going through the red light and striking another vehicle side-on. That vehicle caught fire at once, and the burning wreckage came to rest against a petrol station sign on the corner. According to prosecutors the light had been red for 15 seconds. Early estimates by investigators put the speed at more than 90 miles per hour. Data recovered from the car later showed 122 miles per hour five seconds before the collision and 130 at impact, with no braking or swerving, Deputy District Attorney Brittany Vannoy told the jury. Prosecutors said the recorder showed the accelerator fully pressed.

A Jaguar carrying a young family was split in half. California Highway Patrol investigator Hector Castaneda documented 25 areas of impact. Most reports count nine vehicles in the collision and its aftermath, though CBS Los Angeles counted eight, and nine other people, Linton among them, were hurt.

Witnesses described the scene in court. Veronica Esquivel said she heard an eerie sound and that "it surely sounded like people were dying". She saw a baby thrown through the air and land at the petrol station. Tonya Boyd followed the people who carried the child into the shop and tried to resuscitate him.

Asherey Ryan, 23, was eight and a half months pregnant and on her way to a prenatal appointment. With her in the Jaguar were her 11-month-old son, Alonzo Quintero, and her boyfriend, Reynold Lester, whose age is given as 23 in some reports and 24 in others. All three were killed, as was the unborn boy the couple planned to name Armani Lester. Prosecutors told the jury that the force of the crash tore the baby from his mother's body.

Nathesia Lewis, 43, and her friend Lynette Noble, 38, died in a Nissan. They had been on their way to a shopping mall. Deputy Medical Examiner Vadims Poukens testified that all six died of traumatic injuries, and that the burns three of them suffered came after death. In the neighbourhood they became known as the "Slauson Six".

Linton was on a travelling assignment at Kaiser Permanente West Los Angeles Medical Center. Most reports of the verdict give her age as 41. She was taken to hospital with moderate injuries and was arraigned on 8 August 2022.

A defence motion filed that month set out a history of mental illness. Her family dated it to May 2018, when she broke down while studying to become a nurse anaesthetist in Houston. During a panic attack she ran from her flat, jumped on the bonnet of a police car and was arrested. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and prescribed medication. More than a year later she was committed involuntarily after a neighbour saw her running naked around her building. The motion said she stopped taking her medication during the pandemic.

On the day of the crash, according to the motion, she went home at lunchtime and made a video call to her sister with no clothes on. Minutes before the collision she rang again to say she was coming back to Houston and would soon be married. Her sister Camille later wrote on a family website: "When I see that video, I don't see Nicole driving...I see her mental illness driving." William Winter, a doctor who examined Linton at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center two days after the crash, wrote of an "apparent lapse of consciousness" and added: "She has no recollection of the events that led to her collision."
Prosecutors asked that she stay in custody as a flight risk and a danger to the public. She has been held without bail since.

The district attorney at the time, George Gascón, charged Linton with six counts of murder and five of vehicular manslaughter with gross negligence. One murder count covered the unborn child, because California law does not allow a manslaughter charge for a foetus. "A young family was destroyed in the blink of an eye," Gascón said. Linton pleaded not guilty. Shortly before the trial the prosecution dropped the manslaughter counts, which left the jury to decide on murder alone.

Prosecutors also pointed to her driving record. They said she had no California driving licence, had been in a collision that caused injury in 2020, and in December 2016 had allegedly struck a woman, driven off at about 100 miles per hour and run red lights. In 2022 they said she had been in 13 earlier crashes.

Opening statements were heard on 8 September 2026 before Judge Eleanor Hunter. When prosecutors played the video and showed photographs of the dead, some relatives left the courtroom in tears. Linton, who cried at times, did not testify.

The prosecution case was that Linton hated her job, left it in the middle of a shift meaning to quit, and turned her anger on the road. Deputy District Attorney Antonella Nistorescu said the car's data showed precise steering along the curve of the road as it gathered speed downhill. A doctor who spoke to Linton the day after the crash testified that she at first seemed to remember little, then said her colleagues had made her feel stupid, and that she recalled being angry at people touching her afterwards and upset at seeing her expensive car on fire. Nistorescu said there was no record of seizures in Linton's medical history and accused her of acting out seizures during tests after the crash. "She chose to do this. She did it knowingly and, most importantly, she was conscious," she told the jury. Vannoy said Linton "chose to get behind the wheel of a car and take her anger out".

Defence lawyer Jovan Blacknell said the only real issue was what was happening in his client's mind. The defence said she had not been drinking or taking drugs, was not on her phone and was not racing anyone. A neurologist, David Millett, testified that she had "likely suffered a seizure". He relied on an image showing her arm out of the driver's window just before impact, which Blacknell called consistent with a rigid limb. Firefighter Richard Jimenez said she was in an altered mental state when he reached her. Her sister Kimberly Linton described strange conversations in the days and hours before. "Sometimes a medical emergency occurs while someone's driving. That's not murder," Blacknell said.

The jury began deliberating at 9 a.m. on Friday 2 October and had its verdict by midday. Relatives cheered and embraced as they left the courtroom. "Even though we have justice, grief doesn't change," said Jasmond Nelson, Lewis's sister. Ryan's sister, Shaseana Kerr, said the families would "still all be prisoners of grief because grief doesn't end".
Linton faces 90 years to life in state prison. Several outlets reported that sentencing was set for 1 December 2026.

After the crash the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors called for studies and immediate measures to slow traffic at La Brea and Slauson. On the first anniversary a memorial bench to the six was unveiled there.
